D017-D013_h016.question_both:
I’ve been feeling off for a few months now—maybe longer, I don’t know. Work’s still going, driving the same routes every day, but I can’t stop thinking about how I look. I mean, I’m not weak—I work out when I can, and honestly, my arms and chest aren’t small. But in the mirror, something just feels wrong, like I’m not… enough. I catch myself checking—sometimes in storefront windows, side mirrors when I’m parked. Other times, I avoid looking altogether because it just makes me feel worse.  

It’s been dragging down my mood. I don’t talk to my wife like I used to. I used to joke around with passengers, but now I just keep my head down. I feel tired all the time, like there’s no energy to spare. I don’t know if it’s because I’m down, or if being down makes me notice my body more. I don’t feel like I hate myself, but I don’t feel good in my skin either. Some days I think I’m overreacting. Other days, I can’t think about anything else. It’s not like I’m not functioning—but I don’t feel like *me*.
D017-D013_h016.question_a:
I’ve been feeling really down lately—just no energy, can’t enjoy things like I used to, even spending time with my wife. I know I should be grateful; I’ve got a decent job, a roof over my head, but I just feel broken. The worst part is how I look. I know I’m not small—I’ve been told I’m actually pretty solid, even muscular—but in my head, I’m weak, scrawny. I can’t stand seeing myself.  

I check every reflection I pass—store windows, side mirrors when I’m driving—even the shine on the dashboard. If I see myself, I have to look. But then, once I do, I hate it. My chest, my arms—they never look right. Some days, I avoid mirrors completely because I know it’ll ruin the whole day.  

It’s exhausting. I’ve always been self-conscious, but now it’s constant. I skip family stuff because I don’t want to change clothes where others might see me. I’ve started doing extra workouts at 5 a.m., before my route, just trying to fix it.  

Honestly, I think the depression is from feeling so trapped in this body that just won’t look the way it should.
D017-D013_h016.question_b:
I’ve just turned 41, and lately, I can’t seem to shake this heaviness. I’m on the road most days driving the bus—used to take pride in it, but now I barely have the energy. My wife keeps telling me I look fine, but I feel like I’m falling apart. I used to be stronger, more put together, but now I just feel… inadequate. I look in the mirror and see someone weak, someone who’s lost control—of his body, his life. But honestly, I don’t even check that much anymore. What’s the point? It just makes me feel worse.

I’ve lost interest in everything—my routines, the gym, even hanging out with the guys after shifts. I’m tired all the time, even when I sleep. I snap at my wife over nothing and then feel terrible after. I don’t feel like I’m any good to anyone. My appearance? Yeah, it bothers me, but it’s not like I’m constantly checking myself or obsessed with it. It’s more that I feel broken inside, and that seeps into how I see everything—even my reflection.

I catch myself checking my reflection in store windows, even turning my head just to see the side angle. Sometimes I’ll ask my neighbor, “Does my nose look alright?” or “Do I look normal?”—I’ve asked him three or four times in one conversation. I know it’s annoying, but I need to hear it.  

I’m not sleeping well, lost interest in going to the veterans’ group, hardly eat. I feel like a fool, like I’m falling apart. But what really drags me down is this constant shame about how I look. I feel heavy, slow, like I’m not even myself.

I don’t ask my family over and over if I look okay—I know they’d just say what they think I want to hear, and honestly, I don’t want to burden them. The truth is, I just feel worthless. It’s not that I’m obsessed with my looks—it’s that I feel broken inside, and I suppose that shows on the outside. I don’t care how I appear because I’m trying to hide it, but because I feel too drained to care at all.

No matter how much I lift on the old weights I keep down in the storage room, I still look small, frail—like I’m disappearing. I know, logically, that I’m not built like a boy, but in my head, I’m hollow.
